scope: Read-only causal review of the final lib43/lib69 deployed sample window, before the newly reviewed cancellation-priority source patch is deployed.

evidence: Success advanced once from 13:11:03.133Z to 13:13:03.981Z; count grew by exactly one, so this is one real interval, not a polling span.
nextDueAt remained 13:11:47.852Z at 13:12:20.185Z: already overdue, not moved into the future on restore.
At the 13:12:20 snapshot its raw due rank was 17 of 18, with two global requests in flight. The preceding queue group-008 was cancelled near the same invocation deadline at 13:12:35.528Z.
It resumed at 13:13:02.870Z in the next invocation with no new collection failure.
conclusions.certainty: Confirmed no sample in the 13:12 invocation; bounded-window exhaustion is strongly supported by queue order and the adjacent cancellation. The snapshots do not include that invocation return.deadlineReached or a complete dispatch trace.

evidence: Success advanced once from 13:11:04.704Z to 13:13:28.486Z; one new request, one new success, no new failure.
The original due 13:11:40.690Z was replaced by 13:12:36.528Z together with guardReason=request_cancelled. This guard is returned before HTTP and does not increment request/failure health counters.
Replacing nextDueAt moved unserved work behind other later-due groups. At 13:13:21 it was raw due rank 8 of 14; it dispatched at 13:13:27.338Z.
After success nextDueAt became 13:13:36.528Z, preserving the cancellation retry offset instead of its hash phase 40.690 seconds.
conclusions.certainty: The priority/phase mutation is directly visible in production checkpoints and reproduced against old source. The 35-second fallback is source/runtime evidence supplied by the parent; this report does not infer a per-invocation deadline from status.updatedAt.

exactDifferenceFromPreviousRootCause: The old restore bug repeatedly advanced overdue available groups into future phases. These two groups were unavailable, retained overdue due times through 13:12, and later recovered; this is not recurrence of that permanent-starvation path.

reviewedPatch.behavior: Only request_cancelled retains its unserved nextDueAt; guardUntil still receives retryAt and prevents early retry. Other denial reasons retain original behavior.
reviewedPatch.review: No blocking finding. Fixed, unfixed and minute-aligned modes, cold restore, active guard, default retry, non-cancellation admission equivalence and no same-instant extra dispatch all passed.

coverageLimits: Restoring cancelled priority improves fairness and prevents fixed-phase drift, but does not create extra work time. Had group-008 resumed in the next minute first wave, its preceding successful sample would still have been approximately two minutes earlier.
Therefore neither the 188-second freshness threshold nor this priority patch establishes the 60-second sampling objective.

The scheduler currently waits for both requests in each wave, and normal scheduled scans are bounded to the fallback 35-second work window. Increasing that window needs separate cleanup/runtime-budget review and production validation.

One proven ordinary group (group-031) sampled twice during 13:13 at 02.870 and 33.692 seconds. Its second fixed phase became due after the first overdue recovery; no fast cadence was active. It was last among the 14 raw due entries in the 13:13:21 checkpoint, so this is not evidence that this repeat delayed group-008 or group-012.
The five snapshots do not prove that removing same-invocation ordinary repeats would improve first-pass coverage; do not broaden the fix solely on that inference.
Raw due ranks include possible in-flight groups because checkpoint does not retain per-target inFlight; they describe persisted queue ordering, not exact remaining dispatch positions.
recommendedScope: Apply the narrow cancellation-priority fix with its regressions. Keep 35-to-45-second runtime headroom evaluation separate; do not change configured concurrency or ordinary cadence semantics without a justified capacity experiment.
